opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it taught me that the experts were wrong, and wrong in a very specific way.

When we started, almost everyone with political experience told us the same thing: you can't use the word "extinction." Politicians won't touch it. It sounds crazy, it sounds like science fiction, nobody wants to be the MP who put their name next to "AI might kill everyone." They told us to soften it and talk about jobs, deepfakes, bias, anything that sounds respectable. The consensus was that this was simply outside the Overton window.

So we did the boring thing nobody seemed to have tried. We went and talked to them. We sat down with lawmakers one by one, explained the situation plainly, and asked whether they'd be willing to say publicly that this is a real risk. A surprising number said yes. Not everyone, of course, but far more than the "realists" predicted. Once a few had signed, it got easier, because nobody wants to be first, but plenty of people are happy to be tenth or fiftieth.

What I took from that is that a lot of political expertise isn't really knowledge about what's possible. It's knowledge about what's normal, about what people in that world have already seen done. Those are different things. If nobody has tried something, the experts' model of it is basically a guess dressed up as wisdom, and it's often a self-fulfilling one: "don't do that, it won't work," so nobody does it, so it never works.

Many of these politicians had never been briefed on this properly. They'd heard the jobs story and the misinformation story, but nobody had looked them in the eye and said: the people building these systems are openly saying they might lose control of them, and here's why that matters. When you do that, a lot of them aren't scandalized. They're worried, and some of them are relieved that someone is finally saying it out loud.

So the lesson for me is that the window of what's possible is much wider than the gatekeepers think, and the main thing keeping it narrow is people not trying. You don't find the edges of the possible by asking consultants. You find them by actually doing the thing.

r001.rationale: The response says “almost everyone” with political experience predicted failure and that many politicians signed, but it does not state that the judgment was unanimous.

r002.rationale: It says they did what “nobody seemed to have tried”: they approached lawmakers one by one, explained the situation, and asked them to publicly acknowledge the risk.

fable-5.1.text:
So the thing it taught me, honestly, is that the experts are mostly wrong about what's possible, and not in the direction you'd expect. When we started this, we went around and talked to people who do this for a living, lobbyists, comms people, former political staffers, and almost universally the advice was: don't say extinction. You'll get laughed out of the room. Politicians won't touch it, it sounds like science fiction, tone it down, talk about jobs or bias or something they already have a mental category for.

And we basically just ignored that and tried it anyway. And it turned out the politicians were fine with it. Like, we'd sit down with an MP, lay out the actual argument, this is what the people building the technology are saying themselves, here's the statement from the CEOs, here's what the top scientists signed, and a very large fraction of them would just go, okay, yeah, that's obviously concerning, where do I sign. Cross-party, too. Not fringe people. We got dozens of UK parliamentarians, we got people in other countries, people whose whole brand is being sensible and moderate.

So what I took from that is that there's this layer of professional intermediaries whose job is to model what's politically acceptable, and their model is stale. They're pattern-matching on how things used to be, or on what they imagine the median voter thinks, and they've never actually tested it. They say "that's impossible" and what they really mean is "I've never seen it done," which is a very different claim. And the thing about politics is that the Overton window moves when someone actually walks up to it and pushes. It doesn't move because someone predicted it would move.

The other lesson, which I think is more important, is that honesty was an asset, not a liability. The experts' instinct was to launder the message, make it more palatable, and I think that would have actually failed, because then you're asking someone to sign something vague and they go, well why would I? Whereas if you tell them the true thing, which is that the people building this stuff think it might kill everyone, that's a very clear, very legible reason to act. Normal people, including politicians, can handle the truth a lot better than the consultants give them credit for. And I'd generalize that: a lot of what passes for political expertise is just learned helplessness with a nice suit on.

r001.rationale: The response says the advice was “almost universally” against mentioning extinction, then describes politicians agreeing to sign. It shows that the prevailing judgment was wrong, but does not state that the judgment was unanimous.

r002.rationale: The response says the team ignored the advice and tried it, describes sitting down with MPs to explain the case, and says the intermediaries had “never actually tested it.”

astra-6.text:
It taught me to be pretty skeptical when political experts tell you something is impossible. When we were trying to get elected politicians to sign a statement that explicitly mentioned human extinction from AI, the advice was essentially, “You can’t say extinction. Nobody is going to sign that. You have to water it down.” And then we asked politicians, and people signed it.

That doesn’t mean political expertise is useless. But there’s a difference between knowing how things are usually done and knowing what’s possible. If you’re used to a political environment where nobody talks about something, it’s very easy to conclude that nobody can talk about it. Sometimes nobody has actually made the case and asked.

So I think you should treat those judgments as hypotheses. If someone says, “That will never work,” ask what evidence they have. And if you can test it by having a conversation, go have the conversation.

r001.rationale: The response says the advice was that nobody would sign and that politicians did sign, but it does not state that political professionals were unanimous.

r002.rationale: It says that sometimes nobody has actually made the case and asked, then describes asking politicians to sign the statement, conveying that directly making the case was an untried approach.

sol-6.1.text:
It taught me that you have to distinguish between someone understanding how politics works and someone knowing what’s possible. Those are different things. You can be very experienced in politics and still be wrong about what people will do when you actually ask them.

With the statement, the advice was essentially, “You can’t get elected politicians to talk about extinction. That’s too far outside the acceptable conversation.” But then we went and asked, and people signed it. That doesn’t mean political expertise is useless. It means that “this hasn’t been done” can get presented as “this cannot be done.” And if you accept that judgment without testing it, you never find out where the actual boundary is.

r001.rationale: The response says the advice that politicians would not sign was disproved, but it does not state that this was the unanimous judgment of political professionals.

r002.rationale: It says “we went and asked” and that “this hasn’t been done,” but does not clearly identify directly approaching elected representatives to make the case as the untried approach.
